lesson.title: Coupling
lesson.summary: Understand coupling from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Object Tools & Design
stage.subtitle: Book chapters 5–6
stage.description: Namespaces, attributes, closures, generators, reflection, plus OOP design principles such as SOLID.

payload.markdown: Tight coupling occurs when discrete parts of a system’s code are tightly bound up with one another so that a change in one part necessitates changes in the others. Tight coupling is by no means unique to procedural code, though the sequential nature of such code makes it prone to the problem.

blocks.text: Tight coupling occurs when discrete parts of a system’s code are tightly bound up with one another so that a change in one part necessitates changes in the others. Tight coupling is by no means unique to procedural code, though the sequential nature of such code makes it prone to the problem.

payload.markdown: You can see this kind of coupling in the procedural example. The writeParams() and readParams() functions run the same test on a file extension to determine how they should work with data. Any change in logic you make to one will have to be implemented in the other. If you were to add a new format, for example, you would have to bring the functions into line with one another, so that they both implement a new file extension test in the same way. This problem can only get worse as you add new parameter-related functions.

payload.markdown: The object-oriented example decouples the individual subclasses from one another and from the client code. If you were required to add a new parameter format, you could simply create a new subclass, amending a single test in the static getInstance() method.

items: Coupling: How much one class leans on another's internals; good design keeps it low.
Functions: Reusable blocks of code that take arguments and return values.
Static & Constants: Members belonging to the class itself rather than to any one instance.
Arrow Functions: fn() => expressions: closures with automatic by-value capture.
Data Mapper: A layer that moves objects to and from storage without the object knowing SQL.
Object Identity: === compares instance identity: two objects with equal fields are still distinct.
Static Analysis: Finding type and logic bugs without running the code, with PHPStan or Psalm.
Test-Driven Development: Writing the failing test first, then the smallest change that passes.
